title: Managing family expectations in a special needs trust
summary: Learn how families can navigate caregiver and trustee roles, reduce conflict and create a long-term special needs trust plan that supports a loved one with disabilities.

# Managing family expectations in a special needs trust


####


Learn how families can use long-term planning to clarify roles, reduce conflict and support a loved one


3 min read


#### KEY POINTS


- A special needs trust can provide financial structure and continuity while helping families prepare for changing needs over time.
- Clear communication about caregiving and financial responsibilities can help families avoid misunderstandings and reduce conflict.
- Understanding the difference between caregiver and trustee responsibilities can create healthier boundaries and support better decision-making.


Caring for a loved one with disabilities often brings families together around a shared goal: supporting long-term stability, care and quality of life. However, over time, many families find that the greatest challenges are not financial. They are personal.


As questions around who will provide care, who will manage finances and how responsibilities will be shared change over time and become more complex, conflicts can arise, especially if expectations are not clearly defined at the outset.


“Most families begin with the same goal: making sure their loved one is cared for and supported over the long term,” said[Mike Sears](https://www.bokfinancial.com/about-us/experts/michael-sears) , senior trust officer at BOK Financial®. “But without clear communication, it’s easy for assumptions to take hold. That can create stress later.”


This need for long-term focus is one reason trusts have become more common in estate planning. Sears said many families are more familiar and comfortable with trusts today than they were in the past. That’s often because they’ve witnessed the challenges that can arise when settling a loved one’s estate and want to put structures in place that can help make things easier for the family members who will step in later. Thoughtful planning and open dialogue along the way can help create greater clarity and continuity for everyone involved, not just now but also in the future.


**How roles can change over time**


In many families, parents initially serve as the primary caregivers, financial managers and advocates for a person with special needs. Over time, those responsibilities often begin to shift. For instance, siblings may take on more involvement, and decisions around healthcare, housing and daily support may evolve.


In some cases, one person gradually may become the default caregiver without a clear understanding of what that role will require long term. This situation tends to happen because families have been focused on immediate needs, making it easy for longer-term expectations to go unspoken. The resulting lack of alignment can place added pressure on both individuals and relationships.


“Caregiving responsibilities can become demanding over time,” Sears said. “When roles develop informally, it can leave family members feeling uncertain about what’s expected of them.”


**Where tension can arise**


Even strong families can experience challenges when expectations are not clearly defined, according to Sears. One sibling may feel they have taken on more caregiving responsibility than anticipated, while another may have a different perspective on independence or quality of care. Questions around trust decisions can add another layer of complexity, particularly when authority is not well understood.


In many cases, the issue is not a lack of care or commitment. It is a lack of shared understanding, he explained. Still, whatever their root, these differences can lead to frustration, especially when responsibilities feel uneven or decisions feel unclear, he continued.


**Understanding the roles of caregiver and trustee**


One of the most important distinctions in special-needs planning is the difference between caregiving and trustee responsibilities.


A caregiver is focused on day-to-day wellbeing, including personal care and support. A trustee is responsible for administering the trust and making financial decisions in the beneficiary’s best interest.


“Families sometimes assume those roles should fall to the same person,” Sears said. “In some cases, that works well. In others, separating them can help reduce stress and preserve family relationships.”


When one individual is responsible for both caregiving and financial decisions, it can create added pressure and, at times, tension with other family members. Separating these responsibilities can help establish clearer boundaries and allow each role to function more effectively.


In some situations, families choose to work with a professional trustee or co-trustee to provide administrative support, continuity and an objective perspective—as well as to help avoid potential family conflict. “I often tell people that naming a sibling as a trustee creates a new, and often unwanted, relationship,” Sears said. “The person goes from being a brother or sister to being a banker, who sometimes has to make difficult decisions. Often the sibling and the beneficiary would like them to stay in the role of brother or sister, and leave the financial duties to someone else.”


**Creating clarity through communication**


While no family can anticipate every future scenario, early conversations can help reduce uncertainty over time.


It may be helpful to talk through who will take on caregiving responsibilities, how financial decisions will be handled and what long-term living arrangements might look like, Sears said.


These early conversations can also help family members better understand the trustee’s responsibilities and the reasoning behind certain financial decisions. When expectations are communicated clearly, families are often better equipped to navigate future transitions and avoid misunderstandings.


“These conversations are not always easy,” Sears noted. “But having them earlier can help families feel more prepared and aligned.”


Some families document these discussions in a letter of intent, outlining routines, medical considerations and personal preferences. While not a legal document, it can serve as a helpful guide for future caregivers and trustees.


**Planning beyond the financials**


Special needs planning is often viewed through a financial lens, but its impact extends much further, according to Sears.


A thoughtful plan can help clarify responsibilities, reduce uncertainty and create a greater sense of stability for both the individual and the family members who support them. Just as importantly, it can help preserve relationships during periods of transition, when expectations and responsibilities are shifting.


By establishing this clear framework, families are often better positioned to navigate change while continuing to center the needs of their loved one, he said.


**A long-term, collaborative approach**


Special-needs planning works best as an ongoing process. As family dynamics, care needs and financial circumstances change, plans may need to evolve as well.


For this reason, Sears recommends periodic reviews of caregiving expectations, trustee arrangements and overall support strategies that can help ensure the plan continues to reflect both the individual’s needs and the family’s capacity to provide support.


“Ultimately, planning for a loved one with disabilities is not just about finances,” Sears said. “It’s also about creating a framework that supports the individual and the family as needs, roles and responsibilities evolve over time.”
